clue.text: The girl has merit, says the author

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
to have merit is to be worthy, and with 'has' shortened to 's this gives 's worthy

explanation.surface: Someone praises a young woman's qualities and attributes the verdict to a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'The girl has merit' as 'the gal's worthy': GAL, then 'S (is) and WORTHY, which together spell the name of the novelist of The Forsyte Saga.
explanation.definitionFit: John Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright who won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

parts.note: a gaffe is a social blunder

explanation.surface: An elderly man corrects a mistake he made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' suggests a father figure; in British usage a gaffer is an old fellow or a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is a British colloquial term for an elderly man, from a contraction of grandfather.

indicators.note: the letters of the following word could be made into something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A moral warning that wealth may turn people hard-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sermon about money corrupting; the letters of 'cruel' rearranged give the old word for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money or wealth, especially when gained dishonourably, as in 'filthy lucre'.

explanation.surface: A painter who could perhaps conjure up a breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: James McNeill Whistler was the painter; sailors held that whistling at sea would summon a wind, so a whistler might raise one.
explanation.definitionFit: Whistler was an American-born painter, and one who whistles was believed by seafarers to call up a gale.

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A benefactor who is devoted to music.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'on music' included the link word 'on', which cannot stand in for the answer; the definition is 'music' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form in which a principal theme returns between contrasting episodes.

clue.text: Drink to one female in another Worcestershire town

indicators.note: in places the drink and the female pig inside the second female bird

parts.note: a hen is a female bird, the second female of the clue
ale is a kind of beer
a sow is a female pig

explanation.surface: A toast is raised to one woman in another town of the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' reads as part of the surface but puts drink and pig inside the bird. Worcestershire is a county in the English Midlands; Halesowen is a town near Birmingham once in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Halesowen is a market town in the West Midlands that was historically part of Worcestershire.

parts.note: the film High ... ends in a gunfight at midday, the hour when the sun is highest

explanation.surface: It is well past the moment to open fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High time' reads as 'about time', but it means the hour when the sun is at its highest, the time of the shoot-out in the western High Noon.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is when the sun stands highest, and the western film's climactic gunfight takes place at that hour.

clue.text: Mr. Chips was such an artist

definitions.text: Mr. Chips was such an artist

parts.words: Mr. Chips was such an artist
parts.note: Mr Chips, of the novel Goodbye, Mr Chips, was an elderly schoolmaster, while the phrase also names a great painter of the past

explanation.surface: A claim that the fictional schoolteacher was secretly a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Goodbye, Mr Chips is James Hilton's novel about an ageing teacher at an English boarding school: he was an aged teacher, and the same two words name a great European painter before about 1800.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a distinguished painter of the period before 1800, and read literally it describes an aged schoolteacher.

indicators.note: back says the words for calls and little boy are read together from right to left

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them
Ron is a short form of the boy's name Ronald

explanation.surface: A raider shouts out to a young boy behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the whole run NAMESRON round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Norsemen were the Viking raiders from Scandinavia who invaded Britain and much of Europe.

parts.note: Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's ..., so the small house is found in a work by her

explanation.surface: A cottage in the English village of Stowe.
explanation.walkthrough: Stowe looks like the Buckinghamshire village and stately home; it is Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hut or simple small dwelling is the title home in Stowe's antislavery novel.

parts.note: f, for forte, is the musical direction for loud
the saying 'actions speak louder than words' makes action the thing that speaks loudly without words

explanation.surface: A political group is noisy, and its public-address system is not very talkative.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket '(if un-wordy)' points to the proverb 'actions speak louder than words': a deed is a wordless loudspeaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction is a dissenting group or party within a larger organisation.

clue.text: Incline to join the German club

parts.note: to lean is to incline or slope
der is a German word for 'the'

explanation.surface: Someone is inclined to sign up to a German society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German club' looks like one unit; 'the German' gives DER and 'club' alone is the definition. Leander Club at Henley-on-Thames is one of the oldest rowing clubs in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Leander Club is the famous rowing association based at Henley-on-Thames in England.

clue.text: Woman of the Old Testament, and New, as it happens

parts.note: Eve is the first woman in the book of Genesis
New with Testament carried over from before gives NT, the abbreviation for New Testament

explanation.surface: A biblical woman who appears in both halves of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Testament' does service for both halves: the Old Testament supplies EVE, and 'and New' stands for New Testament, NT.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'in the event' means as things turn out, so the noun stands for how matters happen.

clue.text: Stubborn alumni preserve the tea break

parts.note: OBs, old boys, are former pupils of a school
to tin food is to preserve it in a can

indicators.note: break says the letters of tea are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Stubborn former pupils insist on keeping their tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tea break' reads as the afternoon pause, but 'break' is the anagram signal working on 'tea' alone, and 'the' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstinate means firmly refusing to change one's opinion or course, the same as pig-headed.

parts.note: Jacobite means of King James, and the English colonial settlement in Virginia was named after King James I

explanation.surface: A stronghold of Stuart loyalists in the American colonies.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacobite normally means a supporter of the exiled Stuarts after 1688; here it simply means belonging to James, as the 1607 Virginia settlement named for James I does.
explanation.definitionFit: The first permanent English settlement in America was founded in 1607 and named in honour of King James I.

indicators.note: building means the letters of the first two words are assembled into a new structure

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Walking into a building in some country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' looks like a noun; it is the verb, constructing a new word from ENTERINGA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argentine is a traditional name for the South American republic of Argentina.

clue.text: Youngsters put Cordelia's sister back in the river

indicators.note: in places the turned name inside the river's name

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England

indicators.note: back says the sister's name is reversed

parts.note: Regan is one of Cordelia's sisters in Shakespeare's King Lear

explanation.surface: Young people throw a Shakespearean character into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the sister's name round and 'in' places it inside the river; the Tees flows through north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Teenagers are young people aged thirteen to nineteen.

parts.note: S, south, is a compass point
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone directs attention towards a porch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point to' reads as a verb phrase; 'Point' is the compass point S.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is a covered colonnade or roofed walkway in ancient Greek architecture.

clue.text: Little girl carries a china bird

indicators.note: carries means the girl's name holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: Flo is a short form of the girl's name Florence
Ming is a dynasty whose name is given to fine Chinese porcelain

explanation.surface: A small girl holds a porcelain ornament shaped like a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' says the girl's name holds the rest; 'china' is porcelain, named after the Chinese dynasty, not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: The flamingo is a tall wading bird with pink plumage and long legs.

explanation.surface: Beverages laid on for holidaymakers in summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer visitors' suggests tourists; these visitors are migrant birds that come to Britain for the summer.
explanation.definitionFit: To gulp liquid down is to take it in at the throat, and the fork-tailed migrant birds arrive in Europe each summer.

explanation.surface: Perhaps a past division of a firm keeps archives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former branch' reads like an old office of a company; cut wood was once a branch of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Firewood pieces were once part of a tree, and a ship's or engineer's journal is another sense of the same word.

parts.note: something costing a penny is cheap
wort is the malt infusion from which beer is brewed

explanation.surface: A factory turns out inexpensive malt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory; it is the definition, a herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennywort is a small plant with round leaves, found on walls and in marshes.

indicators.note: returns says the words to and edge are turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a lip is a rim or edge

explanation.surface: A tour guide comes back to the brink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns TOLIP round in one go.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot guides ships through difficult waters, and to pilot is to steer or lead.

clue.text: Blows sounded by John on his trumpet ?

indicators.note: sounded by means the name is said aloud and its sound gives the answer

parts.note: John Knox, the Scottish reformer, wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women

explanation.surface: Blasts blown by a man playing his trumpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trumpet' suggests a musician, but it identifies John Knox through his pamphlet The First Blast of the Trumpet.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocks are blows or raps, such as those struck on a door.

explanation.surface: A beggar, yet one who does not mend pots and pans.
explanation.walkthrough: A tinker mends pots, so one who is no tinker says 'mend I can't', which runs together as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by begging, and someone with no mending skill could say he cannot repair things.

parts.note: a type is a class or kind
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet, as in grade E

explanation.surface: A Herman Melville book rated only fifth-class.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Fifth class' as type E, the fifth in a lettered list; the title is Herman Melville's first novel, set in the Marquesas.
explanation.definitionFit: Typee is Herman Melville's 1846 novel based on his stay in the Marquesas Islands.

explanation.surface: An unknown person's offspring commits a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Diary of a Nobody by George and Weedon Grossmith, Mr Pooter's son is called Lupin; 'bloomer' looks like a blunder but means a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooter's son in the Grossmiths' comic novel bears this name, and the same word names a tall flowering garden plant.

clue.text: " An attachment a la for a bashful young potato" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: An attachment a la for a bashful young potato

parts.words: An attachment a la for a bashful young potato
parts.note: the quotation from Gilbert's Patience needs a Greek philosopher's name in its gap, an attachment in his style being a love without passion

explanation.surface: A line from a Gilbert and Sullivan song with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash after 'a la'. The line from Patience reads 'An attachment à la ___ for a bashful young potato', and the missing name gives 'Platonic' love.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian philosopher's name completes the Gilbert line, alluding to a chaste, non-physical love.

indicators.note: about means the word for uproar goes round the order's letters

parts.note: noise is din or uproar
the Order of Merit is known by its initials OM

explanation.surface: A row breaks out about the first command, and it is nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial order' looks like a first instruction; it is an order of chivalry known by initials, OM.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or foul-smelling, from an old word for harm, not from noise.

clue.text: Quiet girl in charge, and dull

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
Rosa is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken woman runs things, and it is boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet girl' reads as one person; 'Quiet' is the musical P and 'girl' ROSA.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosaic means commonplace and unimaginative, lacking poetic beauty.

parts.note: O is an exclamation used to address or appeal to someone, as in 'O Lord'
men are workers, as in a workforce

explanation.surface: A notice calling on the workforce, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O men!' is an appeal to workers; together the letters give a portent.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign or portent of what is to come.

clue.text: Like the people round one, write calumnies

parts.note: as means like, as in 'as good as gold'

indicators.note: round means the people go around the letter for one

parts.note: persons are people
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Writers like those around someone pen slanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' says the people go around the letter for one. 'write' only joins the wordplay to the definition, the way one might write or cast slurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspersions are damaging or disparaging remarks, slanders cast on someone's character.
